summary: Defines new IKEv2 notification status types so a responder can tell the initiator which address families, IPv4 or IPv6, are allowed. This helps manage IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence on VPN connections, and updates RFC 7296.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8983 lets an IKEv2 responder tell the initiator whether it can give out IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses, both, or neither. This helps clients pick the right request when setting up a VPN tunnel.

questions: how does ikev2 signal allowed address families
subtitle: New IKEv2 notifications let a VPN responder tell the initiator which of IPv4 and IPv6 it will hand out.

tldr.problem: When an IKEv2 initiator requests IPv4 and/or IPv6 addresses, the only generic error is INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE which doesn't explain why a family wasn't assigned or what to try next.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8983 adds IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED notification status types to IKEv2 responses, so the responder can signal which address families are allowed or supported.
tldr.outcome: Initiators can adjust their requests deterministically for IPv4/IPv6 coexistence. RFC 8983 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7296.

today: RFC 8983 is a Proposed Standard published February 2021 that updates RFC 7296. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8983 adds two notification status types to IKEv2 (RFC 7296): IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED. They let a responder signal which IP address families it allows.

The motivation comes from cellular networks (3GPP) which already use cause codes to indicate whether only IPv4, only IPv6, or single-address bearers are allowed. IKEv2 previously had no equivalent way to communicate these constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: When setting up a secure tunnel, one side can now say 'you can have an IPv4 address', 'IPv6 address', 'both', or 'only one of them'.

sections.title: Cellular Context
sections.content: In 3GPP, if only one address family is allowed, the network returns cause codes: #50 (IPv4 only), #51 (IPv6 only), or #52 (single address bearers only). If IPv4v6 is requested but not supported but both families are individually allowed, the host gets one family and must start a second PDP-Context for the other to achieve dual-stack connectivity. IKEv2 needs equivalent signalling.
sections.plainLanguage: Cell phones already know from the network which address types they can use. This RFC brings the same kind of signalling to IKEv2 VPN setups.

sections.title: Why Not INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE?
sections.content: Section 3.15.4 of RFC 7296 defines INTERNAL_ADDRESS_FAILURE, sent only if no addresses can be assigned. It's a catch-all and doesn't tell the initiator why a specific family failed or whether to retry with the other family. This isn't enough for deterministic behavior in IPv4/IPv6 coexistence scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: A generic 'no addresses' error doesn't tell you whether to try asking for just IPv4, just IPv6, or something else. The new flags give clearer guidance.

sections.title: IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED
sections.content:
IP4_ALLOWED and IP6_ALLOWED are notification status types that inform the initiator about address family support/assignment. They carry no data - their presence alone conveys the meaning.

These notifications help the initiator decide whether to retry, whether to request a different family, or whether to start a new IKE Security Association to get the other family.
sections.plainLanguage: These are simple flags. If the responder includes IP4_ALLOWED, it means IPv4 addresses are allowed/supported. If it includes IP6_ALLOWED, IPv6 is allowed/supported.

sections.title: Responder and Initiator Behavior
sections.content:
A dual-stack initiator should include configuration attributes for both address families unless policy/configuration says otherwise. The responder MUST include IP4_ALLOWED and/or IP6_ALLOWED in its response according to the combinations of requested/supported/assigned families.

The initiator must follow: if it receives only one of the notifications, it MUST NOT later request the other family; if it asked for one family but receives the other notification, it MUST request the other family; if it asked for both, got one family assigned, and receives both notifications, it MAY request the other family but MUST create a new IKE SA to do so. Other address-related errors follow RFC 7296 Section 3.15.4.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are straightforward: listen to what the responder says is allowed. If only IPv4 is allowed, don't keep asking for IPv6. If you need the other family and it's allowed, you may request it in a new tunnel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 8983 introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 7296. An observer can already infer a node's address family capabilities from traffic it generates, so these notifications don't leak additional information.
sections.plainLanguage: These notifications don't reveal anything that couldn't be figured out by watching network traffic, so they don't create new security risks.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added IP4_ALLOWED (16439) and IP6_ALLOWED (16440) to the "IKEv2 Notify Message Types - Status Types" registry, both referencing RFC 8983.
sections.plainLanguage: These two notification types now have official numbers assigned by IANA.
